lines: A good harvest keeps a village standing.
I once fixed a scarecrow so well it scared me at dusk.
One frost took half the field and taught the whole village <italic>humility</italic>.
There is a story from the fields, but it sounds smaller unless you were standing there.
Most stories here begin with someone saying, 'It will only take a moment.' They are always wrong.
I remember the smell of rain, the sound of the bell, and everyone suddenly pretending they had a plan.
The funny part came later. At the time, nobody was laughing.
A village story changes depending on who got embarrassed in it.
I could make it grand, but honestly, it was mostly mud, noise, and bad timing.
Still, we tell it because we made it through, and that makes people stand a little straighter.
Once a pumpkin rolled into the square and caused more debate than a council meeting.
I saw a scarecrow wear a better hat than half the village for one whole season.
A storm flattened the wheat once, and every neighbor arrived before I had to ask.
One beet grew so oddly that three people claimed it looked like someone they knew.
A child planted seeds upside down and was furious when nobody could prove it.
The first loaf after a bad winter tasted like everyone exhaling at once.
I once chased a chicken out of the carrots and lost the argument badly.
There was a drought where the well sounded like a judgment every morning.
A trader tried to praise my wheat and stepped on it at the same time.
The best harvest I remember started with a week that looked hopeless.
A fence fell, a cow escaped, and somehow the whole village learned teamwork before breakfast.
I once mistook a melon for a helmet in the dark. Long night.
The field behind the house has survived raids, frost, and my early confidence.
A rabbit ate the prize crop and became locally famous for poor diplomacy.
We once held a feast because the rain finally stopped. Nobody invited the mud.
